transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

Well, hello Doctor. Thank you. I suppose I'm here because I just feel like I’m always up and moving around. Even on a quiet day when I'm supposed to be relaxing, I’m bouncing from writing out the garden club list to digging through my knitting bag, and then over to looking at travel papers before I’ve really finished any one of those things. 

Speaking of travel, my sister is trying to get me to visit her in Arizona this winter. Have you ever been to Sedona? The red rocks are supposed to be just beautiful, but I don't know about flying these days. The airports are such a terrible mess. Last time I flew, they lost my checked bag for three whole days, and I had to buy all new toiletries at this tiny little pharmacy near the hotel. The pharmacist there was so sweet, though, she actually reminded me of my niece Sarah. Sarah just had her second baby, a little boy... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, why I'm here. Yes, I just always seem to be on the go and can't just settle down, I guess.

When you're moving from one activity to another like you described—the garden club list, the knitting, the travel papers—do you find it hard to focus on finishing one thing, or does your mind feel like it's racing with lots of different thoughts at the same time?

Well, it's a bit of both, I suppose. I definitely have a hard time focusing on finishing things. Like, I can start out listening at the garden club planning meeting or, you know, reading the Sunday church bulletin, but after a little while I realize I’ve missed half of what was said or printed. I just drift off. Speaking of the church bulletin, they changed the font a few weeks ago, and it's just dreadful. It's so tiny and squished together. Mildred—she's the church secretary, lovely woman but terribly stubborn—insists it saves paper, but I told her, "Mildred, half the congregation needs a magnifying glass just to see the hymn numbers!" My friend Betty actually brought one of those little pocket magnifiers last week, the kind with the little light built in? She got it from a catalog, I think. I used to love looking through those catalogs, all the little gadgets and things you never knew you needed. I bought a cherry pitter from one years ago, and I don't even like cherries all that much! They're so messy, and the juice stains your fingers terribly. I tried to make a cherry pie once for the church bake sale, and... oh, dear, I've lost my train of thought. Did that answer your question about my mind racing? I just can't seem to keep my attention on one thing for very long before I'm off on something else.
Have you always been this way—bouncy and easily distracted—since you were a child, or is this something that's gotten worse more recently?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask about when I was a child. I've been this way for as long as I can remember, really. Even back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my mother that I was bright but just so scattered. I was always losing my papers, talking out of turn, and just wiggling in my seat before I'd even finished my work. 

Speaking of grade school, I went to this little brick schoolhouse on Elm Street. It's not there anymore, they tore it down in the late eighties to build a strip mall. Can you believe that? A strip mall where children used to learn their multiplication tables! There was a wonderful bakery in that strip mall for a while, though. They made the most divine lemon bars. My husband, God rest his soul, used to love lemon bars. He always said the secret was extra zest in the filling. We tried growing a lemon tree in the sunroom once, but it never really took off. I think it didn't get enough direct light in the winter months. Winter can be so gloomy here, don't you think? That's why my sister wants me to go to Arizona. She says the sun shines almost every day. But as I was saying earlier, the flying... oh, what were we talking about? Grade school, yes. I've always been a bit wiggly and scattered, ever since I was a little girl.
